cards.q: When are the KKT conditions sufficient for global optimality?
pts: The problem is convex: convex objective f, convex inequality constraints gᵢ(x) ≤ 0, affine equality constraints.
x* is feasible and there exist multipliers λ ≥ 0 (and μ) with stationarity: ∇f(x*) + Σλᵢ∇gᵢ(x*) + Σμⱼ∇hⱼ(x*) = 0.
Complementary slackness holds: λᵢ gᵢ(x*) = 0 for all i.
Then x* is a global minimizer — no constraint qualification is needed for this direction.
cards.pit: Slater / a constraint qualification is what makes KKT necessary; it is not needed for sufficiency.

cards.q: What role does Slater’s condition play in convex optimization?
pts: Definition: there is a strictly feasible point — gᵢ(x) < 0 for the non-affine inequality constraints, with affine constraints satisfied.
It is a constraint qualification: for a convex problem it guarantees strong duality (zero duality gap).
If the optimal value is finite, the dual optimum is attained, so KKT multipliers exist — KKT becomes necessary for optimality.
cards.pit: Slater does not imply that a primal optimum exists or is unique, and it is a statement about convex problems.

cards.q: What distinguishes convexity from strong convexity?
pts: Convex (differentiable f): f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) — f lies above every tangent plane.
m-strongly convex (m > 0): f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) + (m/2)‖y − x‖² — a uniform quadratic lower bound on curvature.
For twice differentiable f: ∇²f(x) ⪰ mI for all x.
Consequences: at most one minimizer; with L-smoothness, gradient descent converges linearly.
cards.pit: Strictly convex ≠ strongly convex: eˣ is strictly convex on ℝ but not strongly convex (f″ = eˣ → 0).

cards.q: When is a stationary point globally optimal?
pts: Unconstrained, differentiable convex f: ∇f(x*) = 0 ⇔ x* is a global minimizer.
Constrained convex problem: the condition becomes ∇f(x*)ᵀ(x − x*) ≥ 0 for all feasible x (−∇f(x*) lies in the normal cone).
Nonconvex f: ∇f(x*) = 0 can be a local min, a local max or a saddle point.
cards.pit: At a constrained optimum ∇f(x*) is usually not zero — don't set the gradient to zero when constraints are active.

cards.q: Why is a positive semidefinite Hessian useful?
pts: On an open convex set, for f ∈ C²: ∇²f(x) ⪰ 0 for all x ⇔ f is convex.
∇²f(x) ≻ 0 for all x ⇒ strictly convex (the converse fails: x⁴ is strictly convex but f″(0) = 0).
∇²f(x) ⪰ mI for all x ⇒ m-strongly convex.
Locally: ∇f(x*) = 0 and ∇²f(x*) ≻ 0 ⇒ strict local minimum (second-order sufficient condition).
cards.pit: A PSD Hessian at a single point says nothing about global convexity.

cards.q: What is the difference between a local minimum and a strict local minimum?
pts: Local minimum: f(x*) ≤ f(x) for all feasible x in some neighborhood of x*.
Strict local minimum: f(x*) < f(x) for all feasible x ≠ x* in some neighborhood.
Example: for a constant function every point is a local minimum, but none is strict.
cards.pit: ∇f(x*) = 0 and ∇²f(x*) ⪰ 0 are only necessary at an interior local minimum, not sufficient.

cards.q: What is the duality gap and when is it zero?
pts: Weak duality (minimization): the dual optimum d* ≤ primal optimum p*, always — even for nonconvex problems.
Duality gap = p* − d* ≥ 0.
The gap is zero (strong duality) for convex problems under a constraint qualification such as Slater; for LP whenever an optimum exists.
cards.pit: Nonconvex problems (e.g. integer programs) typically have a positive gap; the dual still gives a valid lower bound.

cards.q: Why can Newton’s method converge faster than gradient descent?
pts: The Newton step solves ∇²f(x)d = −∇f(x): it minimizes the local quadratic model, using curvature.
Near a minimizer with ∇²f(x*) ≻ 0 (and a Lipschitz Hessian) it converges quadratically.
Gradient descent converges linearly at best, with a rate that worsens with the condition number κ.
Newton is affine-invariant, so it is insensitive to bad scaling of the variables.
cards.pit: Far from the optimum or with an indefinite Hessian Newton can diverge — use line search / damping; each step costs about O(n³).

pts: For gᵢ(x) ≤ 0 with multipliers λᵢ ≥ 0, KKT requires λᵢ gᵢ(x*) = 0 for every i.
Inactive constraint (gᵢ(x*) < 0) ⇒ λᵢ = 0.
λᵢ > 0 ⇒ the constraint is active (gᵢ(x*) = 0).
λᵢ is the shadow price: the marginal improvement in the objective from relaxing constraint i.
cards.pit: Active does NOT imply λᵢ > 0: an active constraint can have λᵢ = 0 (degenerate case). The reverse direction, λᵢ > 0 ⇒ active, always holds.

cards.q: When is projected gradient descent useful?
pts: Update: xₖ₊₁ = Proj_C(xₖ − αₖ∇f(xₖ)) — take a gradient step, then project back onto the feasible set C.
Useful when C is closed and convex with a cheap projection: box, ball, simplex.
A fixed point x* = Proj_C(x* − α∇f(x*)) is exactly the first-order optimality condition on C.
Portfolio example: long-only, fully invested weights = projection onto the probability simplex.
cards.pit: If projecting onto C is itself a hard optimization problem, prefer other methods (Frank–Wolfe, ADMM).
